title: Top View of Binary Tree
description_html:
Classic interview problem with no LeetCode number — original source: geeksforgeeks.org/problems/top-view-of-binary-tree.

≈ Closest LC match · 314. Binary Tree Vertical Order Traversal

You are given the root of a binary tree, and your task is to return its top view. The top view of a binary tree is the set of nodes visible when the tree is viewed from the top.

Note:

  • Return the nodes from the leftmost node to the rightmost node.
  • If multiple nodes overlap at the same horizontal position, only the topmost (closest to the root) node is included in the view.

Example 1

Input:  root = [1, 2, 3]
Output: [2, 1, 3]

      1          hd  0
     / \
    2   3        hd -1   +1

Explanation: every node sits in its own column, so all three are visible; reading the columns left to right gives [2, 1, 3].

Example 2

Input:  root = [10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 90, 100]
Output: [40, 20, 10, 30, 100]

           10              hd   0
         /    \
       20      30          hd  -1        +1
      /  \    /  \
    40   60  90   100      hd  -2   0  0   +2

Explanation: columns −2 … +2 are visible as 40, 20, 10, 30, 100. Nodes 60 and 90 also land in column 0, but they sit below 10, which reaches that column at a shallower depth — so they are hidden.

Constraints

  • 1 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 105
  • 1 ≤ node->data ≤ 105

Approach

BFS carrying a horizontal distance (column) with each node: push (root, 0), and for every dequeued (node, hd) push (left, hd-1) and (right, hd+1). Keep a map hd → value and write an entry only when that hd is unseen — the first arrival in a column is the topmost node. Emit the map in increasing hd order (track minHd/maxHd while scanning to avoid a sort). O(n) time / O(n) space.

It must be BFS. A DFS can reach a shallower node in the right subtree after a deeper node in the left subtree has already claimed that column, overwriting a correct entry — unless you also store the depth per column and compare before writing.

LeetCode siblings

  • ≈ 314 Binary Tree Vertical Order Traversal — this scan, keeping every node per column instead of the first.
  • ~ 987 Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree — same columns, but sorted by (row, value) inside each one.
  • ~ 199 Binary Tree Right Side View — one node per level rather than per column.
  • ~ 102 Binary Tree Level Order Traversal — the bare BFS this decorates.

Bottom View is the identical scan keeping the LAST node written per column.
